Question: How many right triangles have integer leg lengths \(a\) and \(b\) and a hypotenuse of length \(b+1,\) where \(b\lt 100?\)
Solution:
The hypotenuse is only one unit longer than the leg \(b\), so expanding the Pythagorean equation makes the \(b^2\) terms cancel:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a^2+b^2&=(b+1)^2\\
a^2&=2b+1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Both legs are positive integers, and \(b<100\), so \(1\le b\le99\). Consequently
\[
3\le a^2\le199.
\]
Also, \(2b+1\) is odd, so \(a\) must be odd, since an even integer has an even square. The possible positive odd values are exactly
\[
a=3,5,7,9,11,13.
\]
The value \(1\) is too small, and the next odd value, \(15\), has square \(225>199\).

Using \(b=(a^2-1)/2\), these values give, respectively,
\[
b=4,12,24,40,60,84.
\]
Every listed pair has positive integer legs and satisfies \(a^2+b^2=(b+1)^2\), so the right triangle with those legs has the required hypotenuse. Different listed values of \(b\) give different hypotenuse lengths, so no triangle is counted twice. The restrictions on \(a\) exhaust all possibilities. There are \(\boxed{6}\) triangles, choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
